questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a data race?
options: Two threads call fetch_add on one std::atomic<int>
Two threads push_back to the same std::vector without a lock
One thread writes a bool, another polls it in a loop
Two threads write the same int without synchronization
questions.explanation: Atomic operations are race-free by definition; the other three have conflicting unsynchronized accesses.

questions.prompt: Why is a std::thread that goes out of scope without join() a bug?
options: The thread keeps running on as a detached daemon thread
The destructor of a joinable thread calls std::terminate
The destructor silently detaches the thread so it finishes
The compiler refuses to compile such a program at all
questions.explanation: Join or detach explicitly, or use std::jthread in C++20.

questions.prompt: A consumer uses cv.wait(lk) without a predicate and sometimes pops from an empty queue. Which explanation is correct?
options: notify_one wakes zero threads whenever the queue is currently found to be empty
pop is not declared const, so it cannot be called while the lock is being held
The mutex was recursive, so the lock was acquired twice by the same consumer
wait can return without a notification, and another consumer may have taken the item
questions.explanation: The condition must be re-checked in a loop or with a predicate.

questions.prompt: if (q.size() < cap) q.push(x); on a shared queue is wrong because?
options: size() is O(n), so the check alone already costs too much on a shared queue
The state can change between the check and the push; one atomic try_push avoids it
push is not exception-safe, so it can never be used on a queue shared by threads
cap is const, so the comparison with it is always stale after any later push call
questions.explanation: Each call locks separately, so the two steps are not one critical section.

questions.prompt: A thread pool counter is incremented 250,000 times by each of 8 threads without a lock and the final value is 1,873,114. How many increments were lost? Integer.
A sensor emits 120 items/s for 0.5 s as a burst; the consumer handles 100 items/s. What is the minimum queue capacity so the producer never blocks (backlog at the end of the burst)? Integer.
questions.explanation: Produced 60, consumed 50 during the burst, backlog 10.

questions.prompt: Backlog is 48 items and the consumer handles 160 items/s with no new input. How many seconds to drain it? Give a number with 2 decimals.
Four threads each run 3 pushes and 3 pops on a queue whose consumers use a predicate. After all threads join, what must size() be if every push is matched by a pop? Integer.
questions.explanation: Items in = items out, so the queue is empty: 0.

questions.prompt: Rewrite 'm.lock(); if (done) return; work(); m.unlock();' so that it is exception-safe and releases the mutex on every path. Explain why.
rubric: Uses std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(m); (or unique_lock) at the top of the scope.
The destructor unlocks on return and on exception.
Mentions that manual lock/unlock leaves the mutex locked on the early return.

questions.prompt: Two mutexes protect two accounts. Write the code to transfer money without risking deadlock and say how it works.
rubric: std::scoped_lock lk(from.m, to.m); then update both balances.
scoped_lock acquires all mutexes using a deadlock-avoidance algorithm, independent of argument order.
Alternative: a global lock order (by address or id).

questions.prompt: A control loop must use the latest sensor reading and never wait for a slow producer. Compare a bounded queue with a latest-value mailbox and choose.
rubric: A mailbox overwrites old values, so the controller always reads the freshest data and the producer never blocks.
A queue preserves every item but risks stale data and back-pressure; needed for logging, not control.
Names a contract: one mutex, set overwrites, get copies the value (and perhaps a version/timestamp).
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: A producer runs data = 42; ready.store(true, S); a consumer spins on ready.load(L) and then reads data. Which pair (S, L) makes the read of data correct, always seeing 42 with no data race?
options: S = relaxed, L = relaxed
S = relaxed, L = acquire
S = release, L = acquire
S = release, L = relaxed
questions.explanation: A release store synchronizes-with an acquire load that reads the value it wrote, so data = 42 happens-before the read of data. With a relaxed store or a relaxed load there is no synchronizes-with edge: the write and the read of data are unordered conflicting accesses, a data race, even if a test on x86 never fails. A release store needs an acquire (or stronger) load on the other side, and an acquire load needs a release (or stronger) store.

questions.prompt: Two threads each run the three steps load, add 1, store on one shared integer that starts at 0 (each thread keeps its loaded value in a private register). Among all interleavings that keep each thread's step order, how many end with the shared integer equal to 1?
questions.explanation: There are C(6,3)=20 interleavings. The final value is 2 only when one thread's load comes after the other thread's store, which happens only when one thread runs all three steps before the other starts: 2 interleavings. The other 20 - 2 = 18 end with 1 (both threads loaded 0, or the later store overwrites with a value computed from a stale load).

questions.prompt: A capacity-1 queue uses one condition variable for both 'not full' and 'not empty' and calls notify_one after every change. Show a schedule with two producers and two consumers that leaves all threads blocked while the queue holds an item, and give two fixes with their costs.
rubric: Schedule: queue full, producers P1 and P2 waiting; C1 pops and notify_one wakes P1; before P1 runs C2 finds the queue empty and waits; P1 pushes and notify_one wakes P2 instead of C2; P2 sees full and sleeps again; C2 sleeps with a non-empty queue and nobody notifies.
Fix 1: notify_all with predicate loops; correct, but wakes every waiter (thundering herd, O(waiters) wake-ups per operation).
Fix 2: one condition variable per predicate (not_full, not_empty) with notify_one on the right one; each notification is useful. State the invariant that each operation restores before unlocking.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
